questions.question_text: What is the definite article of *Kaffee* (coffee)?
questions.explanation: *Kaffee* is masculine, so it takes *der*. Gender is grammatical and must be learned with each noun: *der Tee*, *die Milch*, *das Wasser*.

questions.question_text:
Complete the order "A coffee and a bread roll, please."

```text
____ Kaffee und ein Brötchen, bitte.
```
questions.explanation: The ordered item is a direct object in the accusative case, and masculine *ein* becomes *einen*: *Einen Kaffee, bitte.* Neuter *Brötchen* keeps *ein*.

questions.question_text: The present-tense ending for *du* is built as $\text{verb stem} + \text{-st}$. What is the *du* form of *lernen* (to learn)?
questions.explanation: Stem *lern-* plus *-st* gives *du lernst*. The same pattern gives *du wohnst* and *du machst*; *lernt* is the *er/sie/es* (and *ihr*) form.

questions.question_text: Which indefinite article completes "Ich möchte ____ Milch." (*Milch* is feminine)?
questions.explanation: Only masculine nouns change from nominative to accusative (*ein* to *einen*). Feminine *eine* stays *eine* in the accusative: *Ich möchte eine Cola.* Neuter stays *ein*: *Ich möchte ein Wasser.*

questions.question_text: *Orangensaft* (orange juice) is built from *Orange* (feminine) + *Saft* (masculine). What is its article?
questions.explanation: In a German compound noun the last element decides the gender, so *Orangensaft* is *der Orangensaft*, like *der Saft*. Likewise *das Mineralwasser* follows *das Wasser*.

questions.question_text:
Complete the question "How much does this cost?"

```text
____ kostet das?
```
questions.explanation: The price question is *Was kostet das?* (singular) or *Was kosten die Brötchen?* (plural).

questions.question_text: In a German statement the order is $\text{position 1} + \text{conjugated verb (position 2)} + \dots$. Which sentence correctly starts with *Heute* (today)?
questions.explanation: The conjugated verb must stay in second position, so when *Heute* takes the first slot the subject moves after the verb: *Heute möchte ich ...*. Similarly: *Morgen fahre ich nach München.*

questions.question_text: At the end of a restaurant meal you hand over money and say "Stimmt so." What do you mean?

options.A: That is correct, please check it.

questions.explanation: *Stimmt so* tells the waiter to keep the change as a tip. To ask for the bill you say *Die Rechnung, bitte.*

questions.question_text: Choose the correct form of *haben* in "Er ____ zwei Kinder." (he has two children).
questions.explanation: *Haben* is irregular in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms: *du hast*, *er hat*. The *ich* form is *habe* and the plural is *haben*. Another example: *Sie hat einen Hund.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "I am thirty years old."

```text
Ich ____ dreißig Jahre alt.
```
questions.explanation: German states age with *sein*, not *haben*: *Ich bin dreißig Jahre alt.* and *Wie alt bist du?* Saying *Ich habe 30 Jahre* is a Portuguese-style mistake.

questions.question_text: How do you negate "Ich habe einen Bruder." (I have a brother)?
questions.explanation: *Kein* negates a noun that would take an indefinite article, and it takes the same endings as *ein*: masculine accusative *keinen*. Another example: *Ich habe keine Schwester.* (*nicht* negates verbs and adjectives).

questions.question_text: A yes/no question follows $\text{verb} + \text{subject} + \dots$. Turn the statement \"Du sprichst Deutsch.\" into a yes/no question.
questions.explanation: The conjugated verb moves to the first position and the subject follows: *Sprichst du Deutsch?* Another example: *Wohnt er in Berlin?*

questions.question_text: In a café you say "Ich ____ einen Kaffee, bitte." to order politely. Which form fits and means "would like"?
questions.explanation: *Möchten* expresses a polite wish ("would like"): *ich möchte, du möchtest, er möchte*. It is the standard verb for ordering, followed by an accusative object.

questions.question_text: A question with a question word follows $\text{W-word} + \text{verb} + \text{subject} + \dots$. How do you ask \"Where do you work?\"
questions.explanation: The question word comes first, then the conjugated verb, then the subject: *Wo arbeitest du?* (the stem ends in *-t*, so *du* takes *-est*). Another example: *Was machst du heute?*

questions.question_text:
Complete "My mother is called Maria."

```text
____ Mutter heißt Maria.
```
questions.explanation: *Mutter* is feminine, so the possessive takes the *-e* ending: *meine Mutter*. Masculine and neuter use *mein* (*mein Vater*, *mein Kind*); plural uses *meine* (*meine Eltern*).

questions.question_text: What is the plural of *die Schwester* (sister)?
questions.explanation: Feminine nouns ending in *-e* or *-er* typically form the plural with *-n*/*-en*: *die Schwestern*, *die Lampen*. Some nouns use other patterns (*der Sohn, die Söhne*; *das Kind, die Kinder*), so learn the plural with each noun.

questions.question_text: Which of these German family words is used only in the plural?
questions.explanation: *Die Eltern* (parents) has no singular and takes a plural verb: *Meine Eltern sind nett.* The singular words are *der Vater* and *die Mutter*.

questions.question_text: The perfect tense follows $\text{haben (position 2)} + \dots + \text{past participle (end)}$. How do you say \"We danced all night\"?

options.A: Wir getanzt haben die ganze Nacht.
options.B: Wir haben getanzt die ganze Nacht.
options.C: Haben wir die ganze Nacht getanzt.
options.D: Wir haben die ganze Nacht getanzt.

questions.explanation: The auxiliary *haben* stays in second position and the participle *getanzt* goes to the end of the clause. The last option is a question, not a statement. Another example: *Wir haben viel gelacht.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "Where do you live?"

```text
____ wohnst du?
```
questions.explanation: *Wo* asks for a fixed location: *Wo wohnst du?* — *In Berlin.* *Woher* asks where from and *wohin* asks where to.

questions.question_text:
Complete "Where do you come from?"

```text
____ kommst du?
```
questions.explanation: *Woher* asks for origin: *Woher kommst du?* — *Aus Brasilien.* *Wohin* asks about the destination: *Wohin gehst du?*

questions.question_text: A friend asks "Kommst du nicht?" (Aren't you coming?). You are coming. Which short answer contradicts the negative question?
questions.explanation: *Doch* is the affirmative reply to a negative question, meaning "yes, I do/am". *Nein* would confirm the negative. Another example: *Hast du keine Zeit?* — *Doch, ich habe Zeit.*

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "We must go now"?
questions.explanation: With a modal verb, the modal sits in second position and the infinitive goes to the end of the clause: *Wir müssen jetzt gehen.* Another example: *Ich kann gut kochen.*

questions.question_text: When someone gives directions, which word means "straight ahead"?
questions.explanation: *Geradeaus* means straight ahead; *links* is left, *rechts* is right and *zurück* is back. Example: *Gehen Sie geradeaus.*

questions.question_text:
Complete the instruction "Turn left." (formal)

```text
Biegen Sie links ____.
```
questions.explanation: *Abbiegen* (to turn) is a separable verb: in the formal imperative the prefix goes to the end: *Biegen Sie links ab.* Another example: *Steigen Sie hier aus.*

questions.question_text: Which article completes "Die Bank ist neben ____ Supermarkt." (the bank is next to the supermarket)?
questions.explanation: *Neben* answering "Wo?" (where, no movement) takes the dative case. *Der Supermarkt* is masculine, and the masculine dative article is *dem*. Another example: *Das Hotel ist hinter dem Bahnhof.*

questions.question_text: Prepositions merge with articles, for example $\text{zu} + \text{der} = \,?$ Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: *Zu* + *der* contracts to *zur* (feminine *die Post*), while *zu* + *dem* becomes *zum* (*zum Bahnhof*). Other contractions: *im* = *in dem*, *am* = *an dem*.

questions.question_text: What does the sentence "Es ist in der Nähe." tell you about a place?
questions.explanation: *In der Nähe* means "nearby". Compare *Es ist weit von hier* (it is far from here) and *Es ist nicht weit* (it is not far).

questions.question_text: The formal imperative follows $\text{infinitive verb} + \text{Sie} + \dots$. How do you tell a stranger politely to go straight ahead?
questions.explanation: The formal command uses the infinitive form of the verb followed by *Sie*: *Gehen Sie geradeaus.* Another example: *Nehmen Sie die U-Bahn.* The last option is a plain statement.

questions.question_text: In "Ich gehe in die Bank." (I am going into the bank), which case does the preposition *in* take, and why?

options.A: Dative, because the sentence expresses movement towards a place.
options.B: Accusative, because the sentence expresses movement towards a place ("wohin?").
options.D: Genitive, because the bank is a building.

questions.explanation: Two-way prepositions (*in, an, auf, vor ...*) take the accusative for direction (*Wohin?*) and the dative for location (*Wo?*). Compare *Ich bin in der Bank.* (dative, location).

questions.question_text: Numbers from 21 to 99 are built as $\text{unit} + \text{und} + \text{tens}$. How do you say 45?
questions.explanation: German says the unit first: *fünf* (5) + *und* + *vierzig* (40) = *fünfundvierzig*. The option *vierundfünfzig* is 54. Another example: 67 is *siebenundsechzig*.

questions.question_text:
Complete "three litres of milk".

```text
drei ____ Milch
```
questions.explanation: Masculine and neuter measure words stay in the singular after a number and are followed directly by the noun without an article: *drei Liter Milch*, *zwei Kilo Äpfel*. Feminine measures take a plural: *zwei Flaschen Wasser*.

questions.question_text: A market seller offers "ein Pfund Tomaten". How much is that?
questions.explanation: *Das Pfund* is half a kilo, i.e. 500 g. Example: *Ich nehme ein Pfund Tomaten und 200 Gramm Käse.*

questions.question_text: Complete "Es gibt ____ Garten." (There is a garden; *Garten* is masculine).
questions.explanation: *Es gibt* (there is/there are) is always followed by the accusative case, so masculine *ein* becomes *einen*. *Es gibt* never changes form. Another example: *Es gibt keinen Aufzug.*

questions.question_text: A comparison follows $\text{adjective} + \text{-er} + \text{als}$. How do you say \"Apples are cheaper than oranges\"?

options.D: Äpfel sind mehr billig als Orangen.

questions.explanation: The comparative is formed by adding *-er* to the adjective, followed by *als* (than): *billiger als*. Another example: *Das Fleisch ist teurer als der Fisch.*

questions.question_text: Which verb fits "Das Bild ____ an der Wand." (the picture is hanging on the wall)?
questions.explanation: German uses position verbs: *stehen* (upright), *liegen* (lying), *hängen* (hanging), *sitzen* (sitting). A picture on a wall *hängt*; a book on a table *liegt*.

questions.question_text: Which sentence is correct: "I learn German because I work in Berlin"?

options.A: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich in Berlin arbeite.
options.B: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil ich arbeite in Berlin.
options.C: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil arbeite ich in Berlin.
options.D: Ich lerne Deutsch, weil in Berlin ich arbeite.

questions.explanation: After the subordinating conjunction *weil*, the conjugated verb goes to the end of the clause: *..., weil ich in Berlin arbeite.* By contrast *denn* keeps normal word order: *..., denn ich arbeite in Berlin.*

questions.question_text: Official times use $\text{hours} + \text{Uhr} + \text{minutes}$. How do you say 14:45?
questions.explanation: Official 24-hour time reads the hours, then *Uhr*, then the minutes: *vierzehn Uhr fünfundvierzig*. Another example: 23:50 is *dreiundzwanzig Uhr fünfzig*.

questions.question_text: What does the airport announcement "Der Flug ist verspätet." mean?
questions.explanation: *Verspätet* means late/delayed (*die Verspätung* = delay). A cancelled flight is *annulliert*. Example: *Mein Flug ist 20 Minuten verspätet.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "I lost my luggage."

```text
Ich habe mein Gepäck ____.
```
questions.explanation: The perfect tense needs the past participle at the end: *ich habe ... verloren* (from *verlieren*). Participles of verbs with an inseparable prefix like *ver-* take no *ge-*. Another example: *Ich habe meinen Flug verpasst.*

questions.question_text: Choose the correct auxiliary: "Wir ____ um 9 Uhr angekommen." (We arrived at 9 o'clock.)
questions.explanation: Verbs of movement or change of place such as *ankommen*, *gehen*, *fahren* form the perfect tense with *sein*. Here *wir* needs *sind*. Another example: *Ich bin nach Berlin geflogen.*

questions.question_text: A separable verb follows $\text{subject} + \text{verb (position 2)} + \dots + \text{prefix (end)}$. How do you say \"I get up at seven\" (*aufstehen*)?

options.A: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
options.C: Ich stehe auf um sieben Uhr.
options.D: Ich auf stehe um sieben Uhr.

questions.explanation: In the present tense the verb stem takes position 2 and the separable prefix *auf* goes to the end: *Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.* Another example: *Der Film fängt um acht Uhr an.*

questions.question_text: What does the question "Könnten Sie mir bitte helfen?" express?

options.C: A polite request: "Could you help me, please?"
options.D: A question about the way: "Where is the station?"

questions.explanation: The conditional-like *könnten* softens a request and makes it very polite, together with *Sie* and *bitte*. Another example: *Könnten Sie das wiederholen?*

questions.question_text: Which pronoun completes "Ich helfe ____." (I help you, to a friend)?
questions.explanation: *Helfen* always takes the dative case, so the pronoun is *dir*, not *dich*. Another example: *Er hilft mir beim Kochen.* (*Mir*, dative of *ich*.)

questions.question_text:
Complete "The trousers do not fit me."

```text
Die Hose passt ____ nicht.
```
questions.explanation: *Passen* takes the dative, so "me" is *mir*: *Die Schuhe passen mir gut.* The same applies to *gefallen* and *stehen*.

questions.question_text: In a clothes shop, what do you ask for with "Kann ich das anprobieren?"
questions.explanation: *Anprobieren* means to try on. To exchange something you say *umtauschen*. The changing room is *die Umkleidekabine*.

questions.question_text: At home, what does the verb *abwaschen* mean?
questions.explanation: *Abwaschen* means to wash the dishes (*den Abwasch machen*). Vacuuming is *saugen*, ironing is *bügeln*, watering plants is *die Pflanzen gießen*.

questions.question_text: What is the correct informal (*du*) command for the separable verb *aufräumen* (to tidy up)?
questions.explanation: The *du* imperative drops the *-st* ending and the separable prefix goes to the end: *Räum auf!* Another example: *Steh bitte auf!*

questions.question_text: What does "Am liebsten trinke ich Wasser." express?

options.A: I only drink water when I am thirsty.
options.B: Water is what I like to drink most.

questions.explanation: *Gern* (with pleasure) → *lieber* (preferably) → *am liebsten* (most of all). This sentence says that water is the speaker's favourite drink.

questions.question_text:
Complete the invitation "Do you want to dance with me?"

```text
____ du mit mir tanzen?
```
questions.explanation: The yes/no question puts the verb first, and *möchten* agrees with *du*: *möchtest*. Compare *ich möchte*, *wir möchten*, *ihr möchtet*.

questions.question_text: Choose the correct form of *fahren* in "Du ____ nach Hamburg." (You are going to Hamburg.)
questions.explanation: Strong verbs like *fahren* change the vowel *a → ä* in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms: *du fährst, er fährt*. Other examples: *schlafen → du schläfst*, *laufen → du läufst*.

questions.question_text:
Complete the sentence "He gets up at seven every morning." (*aufstehen*, a separable verb)

```text
Er ____ jeden Morgen um sieben Uhr ____.
```
questions.explanation: In a main clause the conjugated stem of a separable verb sits in second position and the prefix moves to the end: *Er steht ... auf.* The stem must agree with *er* (*steht*). Another example: *Wir kaufen am Samstag ein.*

questions.question_text: A friend asks "Kommst du heute nicht?" (Aren't you coming today?). You are coming at eight. Which reply is correct?

options.B: Ja, ich komme nicht um acht.
options.D: Doch, ich komme nicht um acht.

questions.explanation: *Doch* contradicts a negative question and affirms the action, whereas *Nein* would confirm the negative ("No, I'm not coming"). Another example: *Hast du keinen Hunger?* — *Doch, ich habe großen Hunger!*

questions.question_text: Most adjectives form the superlative as $\text{am} + \text{adjective} + \text{-sten}$ (e.g. *am schönsten*). Which adjective does NOT follow this regular pattern?
questions.explanation: *Gut* has an irregular superlative: *gut – besser – am besten*. The others are regular. Likewise *gern – lieber – am liebsten* and *viel – mehr – am meisten* are irregular.

questions.question_text: Complete the negation: "Ich arbeite heute ____." (I am not working today.)
questions.explanation: *Nicht* negates verbs and adjectives (here the whole action), while *kein* negates nouns that would take an indefinite article. Another example: *Er arbeitet heute nicht.* but *Wir haben keine Zeit.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "We have a dog and a cat." (*Hund* is masculine, *Katze* is feminine.)

```text
Wir haben ____ Hund und ____ Katze.
```
questions.explanation: After *haben* the object is in the accusative: masculine *ein* changes to *einen*, while feminine *eine* stays *eine*. Another example: *Sie haben einen Sohn und eine Tochter.*

questions.question_text: Choose the correct plural of *der Sohn* (son).
questions.explanation: Some masculine nouns form the plural with an umlaut plus *-e*: *der Sohn → die Söhne*, *der Hund → die Hunde* (no umlaut). Others use *-er* (*das Kind → die Kinder*) or *-n/-en* (*die Schwester → die Schwestern*), so the plural has to be learned with each noun.

questions.question_text: A preposition and article merge as in $\text{in} + \text{dem} \to \,?$. Which contraction completes \"Ich wohne ____ Zentrum.\" (I live in the centre)?
questions.explanation: *In* + *dem* contracts to *im* (dative, location: *Wo?*). *Ins* is *in* + *das* (accusative, movement). Other contractions: *am* = *an dem*, *zum* = *zu dem*, *vom* = *von dem*.

questions.question_text: A waiter asks "Zusammen oder getrennt?" What does he want to know?

options.A: Whether you eat here or take away
options.B: Whether you want milk or sugar
options.C: Whether you pay by card or in cash
options.D: Whether you pay together or separately

questions.explanation: *Zusammen oder getrennt?* is asked when you request the bill (*Die Rechnung, bitte*). Eating in or out is *Hier oder zum Mitnehmen?*

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "I love my father."?
questions.explanation: Possessive articles take the same endings as *ein*: masculine accusative → *meinen*. Only the masculine changes in the accusative: *Das ist mein Vater.* but *Ich besuche meinen Vater.* (feminine: *meine Mutter* in both cases).

questions.question_text:
In a shop you want to ask "Can I try this on?"

```text
Kann ich das ____?
```
questions.explanation: *Anprobieren* means to try on clothes. *Umtauschen* means to exchange and *zurückgeben* to return an item; *einchecken* belongs at the airport.

questions.question_text: The informal imperative uses the verb stem without *-st*, but *e → i* verbs keep the vowel change: $\text{du nimmst} \to \,?$ What is the command \"Take the rubbish bag with you!\" built from *nehmen*?
questions.explanation: Verbs with *e → i* in the *du* form keep that vowel in the imperative and lose the ending: *nehmen → Nimm!*, *helfen → Hilf!*, *essen → Iss!*. The prefix of the separable verb *mitnehmen* goes to the end.

questions.question_text: You want to order a drink politely in a café. Which sentence is best?
questions.explanation: *Ich möchte ...* (I would like ...) is the polite standard way to order, together with *bitte*. *Ich will* sounds blunt. Another polite option: *Ich nehme einen Cappuccino.*

questions.question_text: Complete the location: "Der Park ist vor ____ Kirche." (The park is in front of the church; *Kirche* is feminine.)
questions.explanation: A two-way preposition like *vor* takes the dative when it answers "Wo?" (static location). The feminine dative article is *der*. Another example: *Die Apotheke ist gegenüber der Schule.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "Which jacket do you like best?"

```text
Welche Jacke gefällt dir ____?
```
questions.explanation: The superlative of *gut* is irregular: *gut – besser – am besten*. Another example: *Am besten gefällt mir die graue.* Do not form a regular *-sten* from *gut*.

questions.question_text: The existential construction is $\text{Es gibt} + \text{accusative}$. How do you say \"There is no lift\" (*der Aufzug*, masculine)?
questions.explanation: *Es gibt* takes the accusative, and the negation *kein* follows the endings of *ein*: masculine → *keinen*. *Es gibt* itself never changes. Another example: *Es gibt keine Garage.*

questions.question_text: A woman says "Das ist mein Mann." while introducing a person. What does *Mann* mean here?
questions.explanation: *Der Mann* means both "man" and "husband"; *die Frau* means both "woman" and "wife". With a possessive (*mein Mann*, *meine Frau*) it means husband or wife.

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: "Wir schlafen in den ____." (We sleep in the rooms; *das Zimmer*, plural.)
questions.explanation: In the dative plural, nouns add *-n* (unless the plural already ends in *-n* or *-s*): *in den Zimmern*, *mit den Kindern*. The article is *den* in the dative plural.

questions.question_text:
Complete "She helps her mother." (*Mutter* is feminine.)

```text
Sie hilft ____ Mutter.
```
questions.explanation: *Helfen* takes the dative, and the feminine dative of the possessive *ihr* is *ihrer*: *Sie hilft ihrer Mutter.* Another example: *Er hilft seinem Bruder.*

questions.question_text: The perfect tense with *sein* follows $\text{subject} + \text{sein (position 2)} + \dots + \text{past participle (end)}$. How do you say \"He went by train\"?

options.A: Er hat mit dem Zug gefahren.
options.B: Er ist gefahren mit dem Zug.
options.C: Er ist mit dem Zug gefahren.
options.D: Er fährt mit dem Zug gefahren.

questions.explanation: *Fahren* expresses movement from A to B, so its perfect uses *sein*: *ist gefahren*, with the participle at the end. Another example: *Wir sind nach Hause gegangen.*

questions.question_text: You are given directions: "Gehen Sie die zweite Straße rechts." What do you do?

options.A: Take the first street on the left.
options.B: Take the second street on the right.
options.D: Turn right at the second traffic light.

questions.explanation: *Die zweite Straße rechts* is an ordinal (*erste, zweite, dritte ...*) followed by the direction. The command is the formal imperative *Gehen Sie*.

questions.question_text: Which sentence is correct: "I stay at home because I have to work"?

options.A: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich muss arbeiten.
options.B: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich arbeiten muss.
options.C: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil muss ich arbeiten.
options.D: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil arbeiten ich muss.

questions.explanation: In a *weil* clause the conjugated verb goes to the very end, after the infinitive: *..., weil ich arbeiten muss.* Another example: *..., weil er nicht kommen kann.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "Yesterday I called my grandma." (*anrufen*, a separable verb)

```text
Gestern habe ich meine Oma ____.
```
questions.explanation: The participle of a separable verb puts *-ge-* between the prefix and the stem: *an* + *ge* + *rufen* = *angerufen*. Another example: *aufräumen → aufgeräumt*, *einkaufen → eingekauft*.

questions.question_text: With a modal verb and a separable verb the pattern is $\text{modal (position 2)} + \dots + \text{infinitive (end, unseparated)}$. How do you say \"I have to get up at seven\"?

options.A: Ich muss um sieben Uhr stehen auf.
options.B: Ich muss auf um sieben Uhr stehen.
options.C: Ich muss um sieben Uhr aufstehen.
options.D: Ich stehe muss um sieben Uhr auf.

questions.explanation: With a modal the separable verb stays whole in the infinitive at the end: *aufstehen*. Compare without a modal: *Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.* Another example: *Wir müssen morgen einkaufen.*

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "I know him personally"?
questions.explanation: *Kennen* means to know a person or place (be acquainted with); *wissen* means to know a fact: *Ich weiß es nicht.* Use *kenne* for people: *Ich kenne deinen Bruder.*

questions.question_text: Which continuation is correct? "Obwohl ich müde war, ____ getanzt."
questions.explanation: When a subordinate clause (here with *obwohl*) comes first, the whole clause counts as position 1, so the main clause starts with the verb: *..., habe ich getanzt.* Another example: *Wenn die Musik gut ist, tanze ich.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "Although I was tired, I stayed until the end."

```text
____ ich müde war, bin ich bis zum Ende geblieben.
```
questions.explanation: *Obwohl* means "although" and sends the conjugated verb to the end of its clause. *Weil* means "because", and *denn* ("for/because") and *deshalb* ("therefore") would not fit the contrast.

questions.question_text: Adjective endings after *einen* follow $\text{einen} + \text{adjective-en} + \text{masculine noun}$. How do you say \"I take a fresh salad\" (*der Salat*)?
questions.explanation: A masculine noun in the accusative after an indefinite article takes *-en* on the adjective: *einen frischen Salat*. Feminine: *eine frische Tomate*; neuter: *ein frisches Brot*; plural: *frische Äpfel*.

questions.question_text: At the airport the display shows "Der Flug ist annulliert." What has happened?

options.A: The flight is delayed by one hour.

questions.explanation: *Annulliert* means cancelled (*die Annullierung*), whereas *verspätet* means delayed (*die Verspätung*). A connecting flight is *der Anschlussflug*.

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "I like this book"?
questions.explanation: *Gefallen* works the other way round: the thing liked is the subject and the person is in the dative (*mir*). Verbs like *passen*, *schmecken* and *helfen* also take the dative. Another example: *Die Suppe schmeckt mir.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "How much are the eggs?"

```text
Was ____ die Eier?
```
questions.explanation: *Kosten* must agree with the subject: singular *Was kostet das Brot?*, plural *Was kosten die Eier?* The subject here is plural *die Eier*.

questions.question_text: A question with a separable verb follows $\text{W-word} + \text{verb} + \text{subject} + \dots + \text{prefix}$. How do you ask \"When do you get up?\"
questions.explanation: The question word is followed by the verb stem and the subject, and the separable prefix goes to the end: *Wann stehst du auf?* Another example: *Wann fängt der Film an?*

questions.question_text: Someone says: "Ich finde die Jacke zu teuer, aber die Qualität ist gut." What is the speaker's opinion?

options.A: The jacket is cheap but of poor quality.
options.B: The jacket is too expensive but of good quality.
options.C: The jacket is expensive and of poor quality.
options.D: The jacket is the right price and of good quality.

questions.explanation: *Zu* + adjective means "too" (*zu teuer* = too expensive), and *aber* signals a contrast. *Finden* + object + adjective expresses an opinion: *Ich finde die Jacke schön.*

questions.question_text: Complete the reflexive verb: "Ich freue ____ auf den Urlaub." (I am looking forward to the holiday.)
questions.explanation: *Sich freuen* is reflexive and the reflexive pronoun for *ich* is *mich* (accusative). The preposition *auf* + accusative marks anticipation: *Ich freue mich auf den Urlaub.* Another example: *Er interessiert sich für Kunst.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "I eat no meat." (*Fleisch* is neuter.)

```text
Ich esse ____ Fleisch.
```
questions.explanation: *Kein* negates a noun and follows the endings of *ein*: neuter → *kein* (no ending). Another example: *Ich habe kein Haustier.* but *Ich habe keine Geschwister.* (plural).

questions.question_text: An indirect question follows $\dots, \text{W-word} + \text{subject} + \dots + \text{verb (end)}$. How do you say \"I don't know where you live\"?

options.A: Ich weiß nicht, wo wohnst du.
options.B: Ich weiß nicht, wo du wohnen.
options.C: Ich weiß nicht, wo du wohnst.
options.D: Ich weiß nicht, du wo wohnst.

questions.explanation: In an indirect question the conjugated verb goes to the end of the clause: *wo du wohnst*. Compare the direct question *Wo wohnst du?* Another example: *Ich weiß nicht, ob er zu Hause ist.*

questions.question_text: A shop assistant says "Dieser Pullover steht dir gut." What does she mean?

options.A: The sweater looks good on you.
options.B: The sweater is standing on the shelf.
options.C: The sweater is too small for you.

questions.explanation: *Stehen* + dative is used for how clothes look on someone (*Die Farbe steht dir.*). Fit is expressed with *passen* and ownership with *gehören*.

questions.question_text: Complete the question: "____ siehst du?" — "Meinen Bruder."
questions.explanation: The answer *meinen Bruder* is an accusative object, so the question word is *wen* (accusative of *wer*). Nominative: *Wer ist das?* — *Mein Bruder.*; dative: *Wem gehört das Buch?* — *Meinem Bruder.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "We are going to Berlin tomorrow."

```text
Wir fahren morgen ____ Berlin.
```
questions.explanation: Cities and countries without an article take *nach* for a destination: *Ich fliege nach Berlin.* For origin you use *aus*: *Ich komme aus Brasilien.* For a person or specific place you use *zu*: *zum Bahnhof*.

questions.question_text: A comparison of equality follows $\text{genauso} + \text{adjective} + \text{wie}$. How do you say \"The flat is just as beautiful as the house\"?

options.A: Die Wohnung ist genauso schöner wie das Haus.
options.B: Die Wohnung ist genauso schön wie das Haus.
options.C: Die Wohnung ist genauso schön als das Haus.
options.D: Die Wohnung ist schöner wie das Haus.

questions.explanation: Equality uses the base form of the adjective with *wie*; inequality uses the comparative with *als*: *schöner als*. Another example: *Der Fisch ist nicht so teuer wie das Fleisch.*

questions.question_text: A speaker says: "Ich trinke gern Tee, aber lieber Kaffee. Am liebsten trinke ich Wasser." Which drink does the speaker like most?
questions.explanation: The preference ladder is *gern* (like) → *lieber* (prefer) → *am liebsten* (like most of all). So water ranks highest, then coffee, then tea.

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: "Ich wohne in einer ____ Wohnung." (I live in a small flat.)
questions.explanation: After *in* + *einer* (dative feminine) the adjective takes *-en*: *in einer kleinen Wohnung*. In the dative the adjective ending is *-en* after any article. Another example: *in einem großen Haus*.

questions.question_text: Which sentence is correct: "I am not coming because I am ill", using *denn*?

options.A: Ich komme nicht, denn ich bin krank.
options.B: Ich komme nicht, denn ich krank bin.
options.C: Ich komme nicht, denn bin ich krank.
options.D: Ich komme nicht, denn krank ich bin.

questions.explanation: The conjunction *denn* ("for/because") does not change word order: the clause after it keeps the verb in second position. With *weil* the verb would go to the end: *Ich komme nicht, weil ich krank bin.*

questions.question_text:
Complete "I would like two bottles of water."

```text
Ich möchte zwei ____ Wasser.
```
questions.explanation: Feminine containers take the plural after a number (*zwei Flaschen*, *drei Packungen*), unlike masculine/neuter measures (*zwei Kilo*, *drei Liter*). The substance follows without an article.

questions.question_text: The informal imperative for *ihr* is the *ihr* form without the pronoun, as in $\text{ihr putzt} \to \text{Putzt!}$. How do you tell two children to tidy up their room?
questions.explanation: The *ihr* imperative equals the *ihr* present form (*ihr räumt auf* → *Räumt auf!*), and the prefix goes to the end. The *du* command would be *Räum dein Zimmer auf!* Another example: *Deckt bitte den Tisch!*

questions.question_text: At a dance, someone asks you "Darf ich bitten?" What do they mean?
questions.explanation: *Darf ich bitten?* is a courteous invitation to dance. Other ways to ask: *Möchtest du mit mir tanzen?* or *Wollen wir tanzen gehen?*

questions.question_text: Which auxiliary completes "Sie ____ zwei Tage geblieben." (She stayed two days.)
questions.explanation: *Bleiben* describes a state or place rather than an action, and it forms its perfect with *sein*: *Sie ist geblieben.* The plural would be *sind*. Another example: *Das Flugzeug ist gelandet.*

questions.question_text: The half hour is expressed as $\text{halb} + (\text{next hour})$. What clock time is *halb vier*?
questions.explanation: German counts the half hour towards the next hour: *halb vier* (half of the fourth hour) is 3:30. Similarly *Viertel nach drei* is 3:15 and *Viertel vor vier* is 3:45.

questions.question_text: Complete the comparison: "Mein Wohnzimmer ist ____ als dein Schlafzimmer." (my living room is bigger than your bedroom; *groß*)
questions.explanation: The comparative adds *-er* and many short adjectives take an umlaut: *groß → größer*, *alt → älter*. The comparison uses *als*. Another example: *Die Küche ist kleiner als das Bad.*

questions.question_text: Replace the noun phrase with a pronoun: "Ich helfe meinen Eltern." → "Ich helfe ____."
questions.explanation: *Helfen* takes the dative, and the dative plural of *sie* is *ihnen*. Another example: *Ich helfe meiner Mutter.* → *Ich helfe ihr.*

questions.question_text: At a shop counter you hear "Zahlen Sie bar oder mit Karte?" What are you being asked?

options.B: Whether you pay in cash or by card

questions.explanation: *Bar* means in cash and *mit Karte* means by card. Other checkout phrases: *Brauchen Sie eine Tüte?* (a bag?) and *Haben Sie eine Quittung?* (a receipt?).

questions.question_text: A job candidate meets the head of a department, *Frau Schmidt*, for the first time at an interview. Which opening is correct for this situation?

options.A: Hi, Frau Schmidt! Wie geht's dir?
options.B: Guten Tag, Frau Schmidt. Wie heißt du?
options.C: Guten Tag, Frau Schmidt. Wie geht es Ihnen?

questions.explanation: With strangers, superiors and clients German uses the formal *Sie*: *Wie geht es Ihnen?*, *Wie heißen Sie?*. Informal *du* is for friends, family and children, and with adults you only switch to it after the other person offers it. When in doubt, start with *Sie*.

questions.question_text: Compare the pronunciation of *ch* in *ich* and in *Buch*. Which statement explains the difference?

options.A: After front vowels (i, e, ä, ö, ü) it is a soft palatal sound [ç]; after back vowels (a, o, u) it is a rough sound [x].
options.B: It is silent after the vowel u and soft everywhere else.
options.C: It is always pronounced [k], as in Portuguese *casa*.
options.D: It is pronounced [ʃ] in *ich* (like Portuguese *chuva*) and [k] in *Buch*.

questions.explanation: German *ch* has two main realizations: the soft *ich-Laut* [ç] after front vowels (*ich*, *Küche*, *Milch*) and the rough *ach-Laut* [x] after back vowels (*Buch*, *Nacht*, *machen*). Brazilians often replace both with [ʃ] or [k], which makes words sound wrong.

questions.question_text: A learner writes *"Ich mag gern Pizza."* What is the best diagnosis?

options.A: The word order is wrong: *gern* must come before the subject.
options.B: It is redundant: *mögen* already expresses liking, so use *"Ich mag Pizza."* or *"Ich esse gern Pizza."*
options.C: *mag* must be conjugated as *mögt* with the subject *ich*.
options.D: *gern* must be replaced by *lieber*, because *mag* is only used in comparisons.

questions.explanation: *gern* is added to an ordinary verb to say you like doing it (*Ich esse gern Pizza*), while *mögen* already carries the meaning "to like" and takes a direct object (*Ich mag Pizza*). Combining both is a calque of Portuguese *gosto muito*. The conjugation *ich mag* is correct.

questions.question_text: A Brazilian shopper looks for the supermarket section for fruit as a general food category (apples, bananas, pears). Which German word names that category?
questions.explanation: *das Obst* is fruit as a food category and is usually used without a plural (*Ich esse oft Obst*). *die Frucht* is a single fruit or the botanical fruit, *das Gemüse* means vegetables, and *die Wurst* is sausage or cold cuts.

questions.question_text: A colleague says: *"Die Besprechung ist um halb drei."* When does the meeting start?
questions.explanation: In German *halb* counts toward the next full hour: *halb drei* means "half an hour before three", i.e. 2:30. Likewise *halb neun* is 8:30. Portuguese speakers often read it as 3:30 because of "meia" in *três e meia*.

questions.question_text: A Brazilian taking evening classes at a language school wants to say "I am studying German" without suggesting a university degree. Which verb fits best?
questions.explanation: *lernen* means to learn or study in a general sense. *studieren* is reserved for university-level study (*Ich studiere Medizin*), so *Ich studiere Deutsch* suggests a degree in German. *lehren* and *unterrichten* mean to teach.

questions.question_text: Of the following, which is the most formal toast when raising a glass at a dinner with your manager's family?
questions.explanation: *Zum Wohl!* (to your health) is the more formal toast, while *Prost!* is the common informal one among friends. *Mahlzeit!* is a lunchtime greeting and *Gute Nacht!* is said when going to bed.

questions.question_text: Which statement correctly contrasts *schmecken*, *gefallen* and *mögen*?

options.A: *mögen* takes the dative of the person, while *schmecken* and *gefallen* take the accusative.
options.B: All three take the person as the subject and the thing in the accusative.
options.C: With *schmecken* and *gefallen* the thing is the subject and the person is in the dative (*Der Kuchen schmeckt mir*); with *mögen* the person is the subject and the thing is in the accusative (*Ich mag den Kuchen*).
options.D: *schmecken* takes the accusative, while *gefallen* and *mögen* take the dative.

questions.explanation: The experiencer is in the dative with *schmecken* and *gefallen* (*Das Essen gefällt mir*, *Schmeckt es dir?*), but *mögen* behaves like English "like": subject + accusative object. Mixing the patterns produces errors such as *Ich gefalle das Geschenk*.

questions.question_text: Which pair of sentences both correctly express "My head hurts"?

options.A: *Ich habe Kopfschmerzen.* / *Mir tut der Kopf weh.*
options.B: *Ich bin Kopfschmerzen.* / *Mir ist der Kopf weh.*
options.C: *Ich tue Kopfschmerzen.* / *Ich tut der Kopf weh.*
options.D: *Ich habe weh.* / *Mir hat der Kopf Schmerzen.*

questions.explanation: German has two main patterns: *haben* + compound noun (*Kopfschmerzen*, *Halsschmerzen*) and *weh tun* with the sufferer in the dative and the body part as the subject (*Mir tut der Kopf weh*, *Ihm tun die Füße weh*). The verb agrees with the body part.

questions.question_text: A learner tells a waiter *"Ich mag einen Kaffee."* What is the best diagnosis?

options.A: The verb must go to the end: *"Ich einen Kaffee mag."*
options.B: *mag* is fine but needs *gern*: *"Ich mag gern einen Kaffee."*
options.C: The article is wrong; it should be *"Ich mag eine Kaffee."*
options.D: She confused *mögen* (to like) with *möchten* (would like); the polite order is *"Ich möchte einen Kaffee."*

questions.explanation: *möchte* is the polite form used for orders and wishes (*Ich möchte einen Tisch reservieren*), whereas *mögen* expresses a general liking (*Ich mag Kaffee*). Using *mag* in an order sounds odd. *der Kaffee* is masculine, so the accusative is *einen Kaffee*.

questions.question_text: You pay a restaurant bill of 18.40 euros with a 20 euro note and say *"Stimmt so."* What do you mean?

options.A: We would like to pay separately.
options.B: The bill is wrong and must be checked.
options.C: Keep the change as a tip.

questions.explanation: *Stimmt so* (literally "it is right like this") tells the server to keep the change, which is how tips are usually given in Germany: you round up when paying. Splitting the bill is asked with *Getrennt, bitte*, and asking for the bill with *Die Rechnung, bitte*.

questions.question_text: A German pupil proudly says *"Ich habe eine Eins in Mathe."* What does this mean?

options.A: She has exactly one math class per week.
options.B: She received the best possible grade.
options.C: She only just passed the exam.
options.D: She received the worst possible grade.

questions.explanation: In the German school system grades run from 1 (*sehr gut*) to 6 (*ungenügend*), so a 1 is the best. A 4 (*ausreichend*) is the lowest passing grade, and 5 and 6 are fails. Brazilian learners often assume that a low number is bad.

questions.question_text: Which pair of sentences correctly describes a 14-year-old at a Gymnasium and a 22-year-old at a university?
questions.explanation: *der Schüler / die Schülerin* is someone attending school; *der Student / die Studentin* is someone attending a university. English "student" and Portuguese *estudante* cover both, which is why learners misuse *Student*.

questions.question_text: A friend invites you: *"Wir wollen am Sonntag wandern."* What are you being invited to do?

options.A: Take a short stroll around the neighbourhood.
options.B: Go hiking on trails in the countryside or mountains.
options.C: Go on a shopping trip to the city.

questions.explanation: *wandern* is hiking, usually a longer walk in nature, while a short stroll is *spazieren gehen*. Dancing is *tanzen gehen* and shopping is *shoppen gehen* or *einkaufen*.

questions.question_text: A German says *"Ich trainiere im Verein."* What does *Verein* mean here?

options.D: A local club or association, for example a sports club.

questions.explanation: *der Verein* is a membership association (*Fußballverein*, *Schachverein*), a core part of German leisure culture. A nightclub is *der Club* (or *die Disko*), so the two must not be confused like English "club".

questions.question_text: The question *"Wie heißen sie?"* is written with a lowercase *sie*. What does it ask?
questions.explanation: Subject-verb agreement and the pronoun *sie*: the plural ending *-en* in *heißen* shows that lowercase *sie* means "they". The formal "you" is capitalized, *Wie heißen Sie?*, and "she" takes the singular *Wie heißt sie?*.

questions.question_text: Complete the pattern: *"Ich komme aus ___ Schweiz."*
questions.explanation: The preposition *aus* always takes the dative case. *die Schweiz* is feminine, and the feminine dative article is *der*. Another example: *Er kommt aus der Türkei.* For plural country names the dative is *aus den USA*.

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Ich trinke ___ Alkohol."* (I drink no alcohol.)
questions.explanation: Negation with *kein-* (negating a noun with no article) in the accusative: *der Alkohol* is masculine, so the object takes the ending *-en*: *keinen*. Neuter: *Ich trinke kein Wasser.* Feminine and plural: *Ich esse keine Wurst.* *nicht* negates verbs and adjectives, not an article-less noun like this.

questions.question_text: Which version is the standard verb-first yes/no question form of *"Du kannst am Samstag kommen."*?
questions.explanation: Yes/no questions put the conjugated verb first, and with a modal verb the infinitive stays at the end of the clause (modal verb and infinitive bracket). Another example: *Musst du heute arbeiten?*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Das Geschenk gefällt ___ sehr."* (I like the gift very much.)
questions.explanation: The verb *gefallen* takes the dative: the thing liked is the subject and the person is in the dative (*mir, dir, ihm, ihr*). Another example: *Das Essen gefällt ihr.* The accusative *mich* would be used with *mögen*: *Ich mag das Geschenk.*

questions.question_text: Which version correctly says "I invite you to my party" with the separable verb *einladen*?

options.A: Ich lade ein dich zu meiner Party.
options.B: Ich lade dich zu meiner Party ein.
options.C: Ich ladeein dich zu meiner Party.
options.D: Ich einlade dich zu meiner Party.

questions.explanation: Separable verbs: *einladen* splits in a main clause, the conjugated stem takes position 2 and the prefix *ein* goes to the end. It is also a stem-changing verb (*du lädst ein*). Another example: *Wir rufen euch morgen an.*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Die Suppe ist ___."* (The soup is hot.)
questions.explanation: A predicative adjective, one that follows *sein*, *werden* or *finden*, is not declined. Compare the attributive use before a noun, where endings appear: *die heiße Suppe*. Another example: *Der Kuchen ist süß*, but *der süße Kuchen*.

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Das ist ein ___ Tee."* (That is a hot tea.)
questions.explanation: Adjective endings after the indefinite article: *ein* has no ending in the masculine nominative, so the adjective carries the strong ending *-er* (*ein heißer Tee*). Feminine: *eine heiße Suppe*; neuter: *ein heißes Wasser*. (For the accusative masculine you would say *einen heißen Tee*.)

questions.question_text: Which phrase correctly says "Anna's brother"?
questions.explanation: Genitive with proper names: add *-s* directly to the name, without an apostrophe, and place the owner before the possession (*Pauls Schwester*). Names ending in -s, -ß, -x or -z take just an apostrophe: *Max' Vater*. With ordinary nouns use *von + dative* in speech: *die Mutter von meinem Freund*.

questions.question_text: A learner writes *"Mein Bruder ist älter wie ich."* Which correction is right?

options.A: Mein Bruder ist mehr alt als ich.
options.B: Mein Bruder ist älter als ich.
options.C: Mein Bruder ist alter als ich.
options.D: Mein Bruder ist älter wie mich.

questions.explanation: Comparative constructions: after a comparative adjective the standard of comparison is introduced with *als* (*älter als*, *süßer als*), while *wie* is used for equality (*genauso alt wie*). The pronoun stays nominative (*als ich*), and *alt* takes an umlaut: *älter*.

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Ich wasche ___ die Hände."*
questions.explanation: The dative reflexive pronoun with body parts: when the verb already has an accusative object (*die Hände*), the reflexive pronoun is in the dative (*mir, dir, sich*). Another example: *Ich habe mir den Fuß gebrochen.* Without a separate object you use the accusative: *Ich wasche mich.*

questions.question_text: The doctor tells a patient she is on familiar terms with (informal *du*): "Take a tablet!" Which imperative is correct?
questions.explanation: The du-imperative of strong verbs with the vowel change e → i keeps the changed vowel and drops the ending: *nehmen → Nimm!*, *essen → Iss!*, *sprechen → Sprich!*. The formal imperative uses the infinitive stem: *Nehmen Sie eine Tablette!*

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "I stay at home because I get up early tomorrow" (separable verb *aufstehen*)?

options.A: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich stehe morgen früh auf.
options.B: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich aufstehe morgen früh.
options.C: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich morgen früh auf stehe.
options.D: Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich morgen früh aufstehe.

questions.explanation: In a subordinate clause introduced by *weil* the conjugated verb goes to the end, and a separable verb is written together again (*aufstehe*). In a main clause it would split: *Ich stehe morgen früh auf.* Another example: *Ich komme nicht, weil ich einkaufen muss.*

questions.question_text: Use $\text{du-form} = \text{stem} + \text{-st}$, and $\text{stem} + \text{-est}$ when the stem ends in -t or -d. Which pair gives the correct *du* forms of *arbeiten* and *wohnen*?
questions.explanation: Stems ending in -t or -d insert an *-e-* so the ending can be pronounced (*arbeitest*, *findest*, *badest*). Other regular verbs just add *-st* (*wohnst*, *lernst*, *kommst*). The ending *-t* belongs to *er/sie/es* and *ihr*.

questions.question_text: Verb-second rule: $\text{element}_{(1)} + \text{finite verb}_{(2)} + \text{subject} + \dots$. Which sentence applies it when you start with the time phrase *zum Frühstück*?

options.A: Zum Frühstück Brot esse ich mit Käse.
options.B: Zum Frühstück ich esse Brot mit Käse.
options.C: Zum Frühstück esse ich Brot mit Käse.
options.D: Ich zum Frühstück esse Brot mit Käse.

questions.explanation: In a German main clause the conjugated verb is always in second position, but position 1 may be any one element. If a time phrase comes first, the subject moves behind the verb (inversion). Another example: *Heute trinke ich Tee.*

questions.question_text: Profession after *sein* follows $\text{sein} + \text{profession}$ (no article), but with an adjective $\text{sein} + \text{ein-} + \text{adjective} + \text{profession}$. Which sentence is correct for "He is a good engineer"?
questions.explanation: Without an adjective, professions and nationalities appear without an article: *Er ist Ingenieur.* Once an adjective describes the person, the indefinite article returns and the adjective is declined: *ein guter Ingenieur*, *eine gute Ärztin*.

questions.question_text: Subordinate clause pattern: $\text{main clause}, \text{weil} + \text{subject} + \dots + V_{\text{fin}}$. Which sentence matches it for "I'm not coming because I have to work"?

options.A: Ich komme nicht, weil ich muss arbeiten.
options.B: Ich komme nicht, weil ich arbeiten muss.
options.C: Ich komme nicht, weil muss ich arbeiten.
options.D: Ich komme nicht, weil ich arbeite muss.

questions.explanation: After *weil* the conjugated verb goes last. With a modal verb the infinitive precedes it: *arbeiten muss*. Compare *denn*, which keeps normal order: *Ich komme nicht, denn ich muss arbeiten.*

questions.question_text: Equality is expressed with $\text{genauso} + \text{adjective} + \text{wie}$. Which sentence says "The soup is as good as yesterday"?

options.A: Die Suppe ist besser wie gestern.
options.B: Die Suppe ist gut wie als gestern.
options.C: Die Suppe ist genauso gut wie gestern.
options.D: Die Suppe ist genauso gut als gestern.

questions.explanation: *genauso ... wie* (or *so ... wie*) expresses equality, while *-er ... als* expresses inequality. Another example: *Der Kaffee ist nicht so heiß wie der Tee.*

questions.question_text: Possession with ordinary nouns follows $\text{possessed} + \text{von} + \text{dative}$. Which phrase correctly says "the mother of my friend" (a male friend)?
questions.explanation: *von* always takes the dative, and *mein Freund* is masculine, so the dative is *meinem Freund*. This construction replaces the genitive in everyday speech: *das Auto von meinem Vater*.

questions.question_text: The perfect tense follows $\text{haben/sein}_{(2)} + \dots + \text{Partizip II}_{(\text{end})}$, with *sein* for movement and change of state. Which sentence says "I went to the doctor yesterday"?

options.A: Ich bin gestern zum Arzt gehabt.
options.B: Ich bin gestern zum Arzt gegangen.
options.C: Ich habe gestern zum Arzt gegangen.
options.D: Ich bin gestern gegangen zum Arzt.

questions.explanation: *gehen* expresses movement, so the auxiliary is *sein* and the participle *gegangen* sits at the end. Another example: *Ich bin krank geworden.* Most other verbs use *haben*: *Ich habe schlecht geschlafen.*

questions.question_text: Polite requests follow $\text{Könnten/Würden} + \text{Sie} + \dots + \text{infinitive}_{(\text{end})}$. Which sentence correctly asks "Could you help me?"
questions.explanation: The Konjunktiv II modal (*könnten*, *würden*) opens the question, the subject follows directly, and the infinitive *helfen* closes the clause. *helfen* takes the dative *mir*. Another example: *Würden Sie bitte warten?*

questions.question_text: Adverbials follow the order $\text{Te} + \text{Ka} + \text{Mo} + \text{Lo}$ (time, cause, manner, place). Which sentence matches it for "I study diligently at school today"?

options.A: Ich lerne in der Schule heute fleißig.
options.B: Ich lerne in der Schule fleißig heute.
options.C: Ich lerne heute fleißig in der Schule.
options.D: Ich lerne fleißig heute in der Schule.

questions.explanation: The default order of adverbial information is time, cause, manner, place: *heute* (Te), *fleißig* (Mo), *in der Schule* (Lo). Another example: *Wir fahren morgen mit dem Bus nach Berlin.*

questions.question_text: Duration with ongoing activities follows $\text{present tense} + \text{seit} + \text{dative}$. Which sentence says "I have been playing the guitar for five years"?

options.A: Ich werde seit fünf Jahren Gitarre spielen.
options.B: Ich spiele seit fünf Jahre Gitarre.
options.C: Ich spiele seit fünf Jahren Gitarre.
options.D: Ich spiele für fünf Jahren Gitarre.

questions.explanation: *seit* always takes the dative (plural dative of *Jahre* is *Jahren*) and an action that is still going on stays in the present tense, unlike Portuguese *faz cinco anos que toco*. Another example: *Er ist seit einem Monat arbeitslos.*

questions.question_text: Conditional pattern: $\text{Wenn} + S + \dots + V_{\text{fin}},\ V_{\text{fin}} + S + \dots$. Which sentence says "If the weather is nice, we grill"?

options.A: Wenn das Wetter ist schön, wir grillen.
options.B: Wenn das Wetter schön ist, wir grillen.
options.C: Wenn das Wetter schön ist, grillen wir.
options.D: Wenn ist das Wetter schön, grillen wir.

questions.explanation: In the *wenn* clause the conjugated verb goes last; because the subordinate clause fills position 1 of the whole sentence, the main clause begins with its verb (inversion): *grillen wir*. Another example: *Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.*

questions.question_text:
Choose the word that completes the question.

```text
Woher ____ Sie?          →  De onde o senhor vem?
```
questions.explanation: The formal *Sie* always takes the same verb form as *wir* and plural *sie*: the infinitive ending *-en* (*Woher kommen Sie?*, *Wie heißen Sie?*). *kommst* is for *du* and *kommt* for *er/sie/es* and *ihr*.

questions.question_text:
Complete the question.

```text
Was ____ er zum Frühstück?          →  O que ele come no café da manhã?
```
questions.explanation: *essen* is a strong verb with the vowel change e → i in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms: *du isst, er isst*. *esst* is the *ihr* form, *esse* is *ich* and *essen* is *wir/sie*.

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct verb form.

```text
Wo ____ du?          →  Onde você trabalha?
```
questions.explanation: Verbs whose stem ends in -t or -d insert an -e- before *-st* and *-t*: *du arbeitest, er arbeitet*. Without it the ending could not be pronounced.

questions.question_text:
Choose the missing particle.

```text
Ich bringe einen Kuchen ____.          →  Levo um bolo (comigo).
```
questions.explanation: *mitbringen* (to bring along) is a separable verb: in a main clause the prefix *mit* goes to the end. Another example: *Bring bitte etwas zu trinken mit.*

questions.question_text:
Choose the word that fits the translation.

```text
Die Suppe ist ____ salzig.          →  A sopa está salgada demais.
```
questions.explanation: *zu* before an adjective means "too" and signals a complaint (*zu süß*, *zu scharf*). *sehr* and *ziemlich* only intensify, and *genug* follows the adjective (*süß genug*).

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct possessive form.

```text
Ich sehe ____ Vater ähnlich.          →  Pareço com meu pai.
```
questions.explanation: *ähnlich sehen* takes the dative, and *der Vater* is masculine, so the possessive takes the dative ending *-em*: *meinem Vater*. Another example: *Sie sieht ihrer Mutter ähnlich.*

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct verb form.

```text
Ihm ____ die Füße weh.          →  Os pés dele doem.
```
questions.explanation: In the *weh tun* construction the verb agrees with the body part, which is the grammatical subject: plural *die Füße* needs *tun*, singular *der Kopf* needs *tut* (*Mir tut der Kopf weh*).

questions.question_text:
Choose the form that makes the request most polite (Konjunktiv II).

```text
____ ich bitte die Speisekarte haben?          →  Poderia ter o cardápio, por favor?
```
questions.explanation: *Könnte* is the Konjunktiv II of *können* and gives a softer, more polite request than the plain indicative *Kann*. *Konnte* is the simple past ("could" in the past sense), and *Können* is the plural form.

questions.question_text:
Choose the missing conjunction.

```text
Ich finde, ____ Mathe schwer ist.          →  Acho que matemática é difícil.
```
questions.explanation: *dass* is the conjunction that introduces a subordinate clause after verbs of opinion and knowledge (*Ich glaube, dass ...*, *Ich weiß, dass ...*) and sends the verb to the end. *das* with one s is an article or pronoun.

questions.question_text:
Choose the missing pronoun.

```text
Wir treffen ____ um 18 Uhr vor dem Kino.          →  Nos encontramos às 18h em frente ao cinema.
```
questions.explanation: *sich treffen* is a reflexive verb, and for *wir* the reflexive pronoun is *uns*. Another example: *Ich treffe mich mit Freunden.* *sich* belongs to *er/sie/es* and *sie* (plural).

questions.question_text:
Choose the verb that fits.

```text
Ich ____ zweimal pro Woche schwimmen.          →  Vou nadar duas vezes por semana.
```
questions.explanation: Activities away from home are expressed with *gehen* + infinitive: *schwimmen gehen*, *wandern gehen*, *tanzen gehen*. *machen* is used with nouns (*Yoga machen*) and *spielen* with games and instruments (*Fußball spielen*).

questions.question_text: A bottle in a laboratory carries the label *"Vorsicht: Gift!"* A Brazilian colleague who knows the English word "gift" assumes it is a present. What should the colleague understand?

options.A: It is a prescription for a medicine.
options.B: It is a warning: *Gift* means poison.
options.C: It is a gift that must be handled carefully.
options.D: It is a note that the bottle is a free sample.

questions.explanation: *das Gift* is poison; a present is *das Geschenk*. This is a classic false friend with English "gift". Related traps: *der Rat* is advice (not a council) and *das Rezept* is both a prescription and a cooking recipe.

questions.question_text: In a café a customer says to the waiter: *"Ich will einen Kaffee."* What is the problem?

options.A: It is grammatical but sounds blunt and demanding; *"Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte."* or *"Ich hätte gern einen Kaffee."* is the polite register.
options.B: It is wrong because *ich will* is only used in the past tense.
options.C: It is too polite for a café and should be replaced by *"Gib mir einen Kaffee."*
options.D: It is ungrammatical, because *wollen* cannot be used with a noun object.

questions.explanation: *wollen* expresses a firm wish and, in a service situation, comes across as impolite. Politeness is built with the Konjunktiv II forms *möchte*, *hätte gern*, *könnte ich ... haben?* and with *bitte*. The imperative *Gib mir ...* is even more direct.

questions.question_text: A Brazilian, translating "Eu tenho 25 anos" word for word, says *"Ich habe 25 Jahre."* Which is the natural German way to state age?
questions.explanation: German expresses age with *sein* (and usually *alt*), not with *haben*: *Ich bin 25 Jahre alt*, *Wie alt bist du?*. The calque *Ich habe 25 Jahre* from Portuguese *ter* is a common mistake. The same applies to *Mir ist kalt* instead of "I have cold".

questions.question_text: On a cold day a Brazilian wants to say "I am cold" in the sense of feeling cold, translating "Estou com frio". Which sentence is the idiomatic choice?
questions.explanation: Physical sensations of temperature use a dative construction: *Mir ist kalt / warm / heiß / schlecht*. *Ich bin kalt* describes a cold person (unfriendly, or cold to the touch), not how you feel. The accusative *Mich ist* is ungrammatical.

questions.question_text: You ask a German colleague *"Wie geht's?"* and receive the answer *"Es geht."* How should you interpret it?

options.D: I do not understand the question.

questions.explanation: *Es geht* (literally "it goes") is a reserved answer meaning "so-so", close to *nicht so gut* but milder. Positive answers are *Gut, danke* or *Sehr gut*. Portuguese speakers often hear it as the positive "vai indo", but it is more lukewarm.

questions.question_text: At 12:30 a colleague you pass in an office corridor says *"Mahlzeit!"* What is the most natural reaction?
questions.explanation: *Mahlzeit!* is a casual greeting used around lunchtime in many German workplaces, with a wish for a good meal, and the usual reply is simply *Mahlzeit!* (or *Danke, gleichfalls*). *Gute Nacht* is only said when going to sleep, and *Prost* is a toast.

questions.question_text: You write a first email to a landlord whose name you know (*Herr Müller*) but whom you have never met. Which opening is the best choice?

options.A: Hallo Müller, ich interessiere mich für deine Wohnung.
options.B: Sehr geehrter Herr Müller, ich interessiere mich für deine Wohnung.
options.C: Hi Herr Müller, ich interessiere mich für deine Wohnung.
options.D: Sehr geehrter Herr Müller, ich interessiere mich für Ihre Wohnung.

questions.explanation: A formal first contact calls for a formal salutation and consistent *Sie* forms (*Ihre Wohnung*, *Ihnen*). Mixing registers, such as a formal salutation with *deine*, looks careless, and *du* should only be used after it has been offered.

questions.question_text: Which study method is the most effective for remembering which verbs take the dative (*helfen*, *danken*, *gratulieren*, *gefallen*, *schmecken*)?

options.A: Postpone case until the vocabulary is complete, because Germans understand you anyway.
options.B: Assume that every verb of feeling takes the accusative.
options.C: Learn each verb inside a short model sentence with a dative pronoun, such as *Ich helfe dir* or *Das gefällt mir*, and repeat it aloud.
options.D: Memorize only the Portuguese translations, because the case follows from the meaning.

questions.explanation: Case government is arbitrary, so it has to be memorized together with the verb. Chunks such as *Ich danke dir* train the pattern and the pronoun at once. Portuguese translations are misleading: *ajudar* takes a direct object, while *helfen* takes the dative.

questions.question_text: A Brazilian learner keeps choosing the wrong article. Which strategy prevents the most errors in the long run?

options.A: Learn only the noun and add articles later by feel.
options.B: Copy the gender of the Portuguese word, because the genders usually match.
options.C: Learn every noun together with its article (and plural), for example *der Käse*, *die Sonne*, *das Brot*.
options.D: Use *der* for every noun until a native speaker corrects you.

questions.explanation: Gender is part of the noun and has to be stored with it. Genders often differ from Portuguese: *o queijo* (masc.) is *der Käse*, but *o sol* is *die Sonne* and *a lua* is *der Mond*. Learning bare nouns causes case and adjective-ending errors later.

questions.question_text: A learner keeps writing *"Ich komme nicht, weil ich bin krank."* Which mental rule best fixes the habit?

options.A: Use *weil* only in the past tense.
options.B: Link *weil*, *dass* and *wenn* with verb-final order; use *denn* (or a new sentence) when you want ordinary main-clause order.
options.C: Always put the verb right after *weil*, because it is a coordinating conjunction.
options.D: Drop the comma and the problem disappears.

questions.explanation: *weil* introduces a subordinate clause, which sends the conjugated verb to the end: *..., weil ich krank bin*. *denn* is a coordinating conjunction and keeps main-clause order: *..., denn ich bin krank*. Treating them as identical is a common transfer from Portuguese *porque*.

questions.question_text: In which sentence is *wann* the correct choice?

options.B: Wann es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.
options.D: Wann ich Zeit habe, rufe ich dich an.

questions.explanation: *wann* is the question word "at what time?", while *wenn* is a conjunction meaning "if" or "whenever". A conditional or repeated-event clause uses *wenn*: *Wenn es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.* Portuguese uses *quando* for both, which causes confusion.

questions.question_text: A colleague sneezes in the meeting room. What do you say in German?
questions.explanation: *Gesundheit!* is the standard reaction to a sneeze. *Gute Besserung!* is wished to someone who is ill or injured, *Guten Appetit!* before a meal and *Viel Erfolg!* before an exam or a task.

questions.question_text: Which word names a male nurse in German?
questions.explanation: The traditional word for a nurse is *die Krankenschwester* (literally "sick-sister"), a female form with no *-in* suffix. For a man the title is *der Krankenpfleger* (female: *die Krankenpflegerin*). Most other professions form the feminine with *-in*: *Lehrer → Lehrerin*.

questions.question_text: At the end of a meal in a restaurant, what is the clear way to ask for the bill?
questions.explanation: *die Rechnung* is the bill. *die Karte* is ambiguous (menu, card, map, ticket) and usually means the menu in a restaurant, *das Trinkgeld* is the tip and *das Rezept* is a prescription or a recipe.

questions.question_text: Which pair of greetings is typical of southern Germany and Austria?
questions.explanation: *Servus* (informal, hello or goodbye) and *Grüß Gott* (hello) are regional greetings of Bavaria and Austria. *Guten Tag*, *Hallo* and *Tschüss* work everywhere, and *Guten Abend* and *Gute Nacht* are tied to the time of day.

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly negates *"Sie kommt aus Spanien."*?
questions.explanation: Negation with *nicht*: it follows the conjugated verb and stands before the phrase it negates (a place, a prepositional phrase or an adjective). *kein-* only negates nouns. Another example: *Wir wohnen nicht in Wien.*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Sie ___ sehr gut Deutsch."* (She speaks German very well.)
questions.explanation: Present tense of the strong verb *sprechen*: the vowel changes e → i in the *du* and *er/sie/es* forms, so *sie spricht*. *du sprichst* is the second person, and *ihr sprecht* keeps the original vowel. Another example: *Er isst Fisch.*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Er ___ heute lange arbeiten."* (He has to work late today.)
questions.explanation: Present tense of the modal verb *müssen*: *ich* and *er/sie/es* share the same form without an ending (*ich muss, er muss*), and the main verb goes to the end as an infinitive. *du musst* is the second person. Another example: *Sie kann gut kochen.*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Ich helfe ___."* (I help him.)
questions.explanation: The verb *helfen* takes the dative, so the pronoun is *ihm* (him), *ihr* (her), *dir* (you). The accusative *ihn* is used with verbs like *sehen* or *einladen*: *Ich sehe ihn.* Another dative verb: *Ich danke dir.*

questions.question_text: Which sentence correctly says "I find the cake too sweet"?

options.A: Ich finde den Kuchen zu süßer.
options.B: Ich finde den Kuchen zu süß.
options.C: Ich finde dem Kuchen zu süß.
options.D: Ich finde der Kuchen zu süß.

questions.explanation: In the opinion pattern *finden + object + adjective* the object is in the accusative (*der Kuchen → den Kuchen*) and the predicative adjective is not declined. Another example: *Ich finde die Suppe lecker.*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Ich rufe ___ Schwester an."* (I call my sister.)
questions.explanation: The verb *anrufen* takes the accusative, and in the feminine singular the accusative possessive is identical to the nominative: *meine Schwester*. Compare the dative verb *helfen*: *Ich helfe meiner Schwester.* Masculine accusative: *Ich rufe meinen Bruder an.*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Ich ___ schlecht geschlafen."* (I slept badly.)
questions.explanation: Choice of auxiliary in the perfect tense: most verbs, including *schlafen*, form it with *haben* (*Ich habe geschlafen*). Verbs of movement or change of state use *sein* (*Ich bin aufgestanden*, *Er ist krank geworden*).

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence to give gentle advice: *"Du ___ zum Arzt gehen."*
questions.explanation: Konjunktiv II of the modal verb *sollen* gives advice politely: *ich sollte, du solltest, wir sollten*. The plain present *du sollst* sounds like an order. Another example: *Sie sollten viel Wasser trinken.*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Ich fahre mit ___ Bus zur Schule."*
questions.explanation: The preposition *mit* always takes the dative. *der Bus* is masculine, so the dative article is *dem*. Note also *zur* = *zu der* (feminine dative of *die Schule*). Another example: *Wir fahren mit dem Rad.*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Ich habe die Prüfung ___."* (I passed the exam.)
questions.explanation: Participles of verbs with an inseparable prefix (*be-, ver-, ent-, er-, ge-, zer-*) take no *ge-*: *bestehen → bestanden*, *verstehen → verstanden*, *besuchen → besucht*. Separable verbs insert it: *anrufen → angerufen*.

questions.question_text: Complete the question: *"___ gehst du am Wochenende? — Ins Kino."*
questions.explanation: German distinguishes *wo* (where, location), *wohin* (where to, direction) and *woher* (where from). The answer *Ins Kino* names a direction, so the question is *Wohin gehst du?* Another example: *Woher kommst du? — Aus Brasilien.*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Es ___ morgen regnen."* (It will rain tomorrow.)
questions.explanation: The future with *werden* + infinitive at the end: *ich werde, du wirst, er/sie/es wird, wir werden*. In everyday speech the present with a time word is more common: *Morgen regnet es.* Another example: *Wir werden wandern.*

questions.question_text: Complete the sentence: *"Er spielt ___ als ich."* (He plays better than I do.)
questions.explanation: Irregular comparatives: *gut → besser → am besten*, just like *gern → lieber → am liebsten* and *viel → mehr*. Regular comparatives add *-er*: *süß → süßer*. After the comparative comes *als*: *besser als ich*.

questions.question_text: Verb-second rule: $\text{element}_{(1)} + V_{(2)} + \text{subject} + \dots$. Which sentence puts the object *Pizza* in first position for emphasis, meaning "Pizza, I like to eat"?
questions.explanation: Any single element may occupy position 1, even the object, but the conjugated verb must stay in position 2, so the subject follows it. Another example: *Fisch mag ich nicht.*

questions.question_text: Object order follows $\text{Akk-pronoun} + \text{Dat-noun}$ when one object is a pronoun, but $\text{Dat-noun} + \text{Akk-noun}$ with two nouns. Which sentence is correct?
questions.explanation: A pronoun object precedes a noun object, whatever its case. With two nouns the dative comes first: *Ich gebe dem Lehrer das Buch.* The teacher is the recipient, so *der Lehrer* is dative: *dem Lehrer*.

questions.question_text: Subordinate clause in the perfect tense: $\dots, \text{weil} + S + \dots + \text{Partizip II} + \text{haben}_{\text{fin}}$. Which sentence is correct?

options.A: Ich bin glücklich, weil ich die Prüfung habe bestanden.
options.B: Ich bin glücklich, weil ich habe die Prüfung bestanden.
options.C: Ich bin glücklich, weil ich bestanden habe die Prüfung.
options.D: Ich bin glücklich, weil ich die Prüfung bestanden habe.

questions.explanation: In a subordinate clause both verb parts go to the end, with the conjugated auxiliary last: *bestanden habe*. Another example: *Ich weiß, dass er gestern angerufen hat.*

questions.question_text: For regular separable verbs the participle is $\text{prefix} + \text{ge} + \text{stem} + \text{-t}$. What is the participle of *einkaufen*?
questions.explanation: The *ge-* is inserted between the separable prefix and the stem: *ein + ge + kauf + t*. Compare *anrufen → angerufen*, *aufräumen → aufgeräumt*. Inseparable verbs have no *ge-*: *besuchen → besucht*.

questions.question_text: Spoken time follows $\text{Viertel vor} + (h+1)$ for quarter to the next hour. How is 14:45 said in the 12-hour spoken style?
questions.explanation: A quarter before three is *Viertel vor drei* (14:45); *Viertel nach zwei* is 14:15 and *halb drei* is 14:30. Rule: *vor* and *halb* point to the next hour.

questions.question_text: Feminine professions form the plural with $\text{-in} \to \text{-innen}$. What is the plural of *die Köchin* (female cook)?
questions.explanation: The feminine suffix *-in* doubles its final consonant before the plural ending: *Lehrerin → Lehrerinnen*, *Ärztin → Ärztinnen*, *Studentin → Studentinnen*.

questions.question_text: Frequency follows $\text{number} + \text{-mal} + \text{pro/im} + \text{time unit}$. Which phrase says "twice a month"?
questions.explanation: *im* = *in dem* (dative, masculine *der Monat*): *zweimal im Monat*. With a week you can also use *pro*: *dreimal pro Woche*. For the day of the week the pattern is *am*: *am Montag*.

questions.question_text: Comparatives add an umlaut to short adjectives with a, o, u: $\text{Adj}_{a/o/u} \to \ddot{a}/\ddot{o}/\ddot{u} + \text{-er}$. Which sentence says "The curry is spicier than the goulash"?

options.A: Das Curry ist scharfer als das Gulasch.
options.B: Das Curry ist schärfer wie das Gulasch.
options.C: Das Curry ist schärfer als das Gulasch.
options.D: Das Curry ist scharfer wie das Gulasch.

questions.explanation: Many one-syllable adjectives with a, o or u add an umlaut in the comparative: *alt → älter*, *jung → jünger*, *warm → wärmer*, *scharf → schärfer*. The comparison is introduced with *als*, not *wie*.

questions.question_text: Preference follows the sequence $\text{gern} \to \text{lieber} \to \text{am liebsten}$. Which sentence says that tea is what you like to drink most of all?
questions.explanation: The adverb *gern* has irregular degrees: *gern, lieber, am liebsten*. Another example: *Ich trinke lieber Tee als Kaffee.* The forms *gernster* or *mehr gern* do not exist.

questions.question_text: The *du* ending is $\text{stem} + \text{-st}$, but stems ending in -s, -ß or -z take only $\text{stem} + \text{-t}$. Which row gives the correct *du* forms of *heißen*, *reisen* and *sitzen*?

options.A: du heißst, du reisst, du sitzst
options.B: du heißen, du reisen, du sitzen
options.C: du heißt, du reist, du sitzt
options.D: du heißet, du reiset, du sitzet

questions.explanation: After a sibilant (s, ß, z) the ending *-st* would merge, so the *du* form is the same as the *er/sie/es* form: *du heißt, du isst, du tanzt*. Stems in -t or -d add -e-: *du arbeitest*.

questions.question_text: Contractions follow $\text{in} + \text{das} \to \text{ins}$ (direction, accusative) and $\text{in} + \text{dem} \to \text{im}$ (location, dative). Which pair of sentences is correct?

options.A: Wir gehen ins Kino. / Ich arbeite ins Büro.
options.B: Wir gehen ins Kino. / Ich arbeite im Büro.
options.C: Wir gehen im Kino. / Ich arbeite im Büro.
options.D: Wir gehen im Kino. / Ich arbeite ins Büro.

questions.explanation: With two-way prepositions like *in*, motion toward a place takes the accusative (*ins Kino gehen*) and a position takes the dative (*im Büro arbeiten*). Another pair: *Ich gehe in die Schule* but *Ich bin in der Schule*.

questions.question_text:
Choose the polite form.

```text
Wir ____ gern die Rechnung.          →  Gostaríamos da conta.
```
questions.explanation: *Wir hätten gern ...* uses the Konjunktiv II of *haben* for polite requests. *hatten* is the simple past ("we had"), *hätte* is the form for *ich* and *er/sie/es*, and *haben* alone does not mean "would like".

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct pronoun for a formal question from a waiter to a guest.

```text
Wie schmeckt es ____ ?          →  Está gostoso para o senhor?
```
questions.explanation: *schmecken* takes the dative, and the formal *Sie* has the dative *Ihnen* (capitalized). The informal equivalent is *Schmeckt es dir?* *Sie* would be the nominative or accusative.

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct pronoun.

```text
Ich habe ____ den Fuß gebrochen.          →  Quebrei o pé.
```
questions.explanation: When a body part is the direct object, the person is expressed with a dative reflexive pronoun: *Ich habe mir den Fuß gebrochen*, *Ich wasche mir die Hände*. The body part carries the definite article, not a possessive.

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct article.

```text
Sie ist ____ sehr gute Ärztin.          →  Ela é uma médica muito boa.
```
questions.explanation: A profession has no article after *sein* (*Sie ist Ärztin*), but once an adjective is added the indefinite article returns, in the nominative feminine: *eine sehr gute Ärztin*. The masculine would be *ein sehr guter Arzt*.

questions.question_text:
Choose the contracted preposition.

```text
Wir fahren mit dem Rad ____ See.          →  Vamos de bicicleta ao lago.
```
questions.explanation: *zu* takes the dative and merges with *dem* into *zum* (*zu dem See*, masculine). The feminine would be *zur* (*zur Schule*). *nach* is used with countries and cities, and *zu* alone needs an article here.

questions.question_text:
Choose the right comparison word.

```text
Sie sieht aus ____ ihre Mutter.          →  Ela se parece com a mãe.
```
questions.explanation: *aussehen wie* is the fixed construction for "to look like". *als* is only used after comparatives (*älter als*) or with roles (*Ich arbeite als Koch*). Another example: *Er sieht aus wie sein Vater.*

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct preposition (the speaker still lives there).

```text
Ich lebe ____ 2015 in Berlin.          →  Moro em Berlim desde 2015.
```
questions.explanation: *seit* + a starting point (a year or a duration in the dative) combines with the present tense for something still true: *Ich lebe seit 2015 in Berlin.* *vor* means "ago" (*vor drei Jahren*), *für* describes a planned duration and *bis* gives an end point.

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct verb form.

```text
Hast du Lust, mit mir zu ____ ?          →  Quer correr comigo?
```
questions.explanation: After *zu* an infinitive clause needs the infinitive: *Lust haben, ... zu joggen*. The infinitive clause is separated by a comma. Another example: *Hast du Lust, ins Kino zu gehen?*

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct form.

```text
Darf ich mit Karte ____ ?          →  Posso pagar com cartão?
```
questions.explanation: A modal verb (*dürfen*, *können*, *müssen*) is followed by the plain infinitive at the end of the clause, without *zu*: *Darf ich mit Karte bezahlen?* Another example: *Ich muss heute arbeiten.*

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct past form.

```text
Die Party war toll! Wir ____ viel Spaß.          →  A festa foi ótima! Nos divertimos muito.
```
questions.explanation: Simple past (Präteritum) of *haben* for *wir*: *wir hatten* (*ich hatte, du hattest, er hatte*). The idiom is *Spaß haben* (not *sein*). *hätten* is the Konjunktiv II form and *hatte* would need the subject *ich* or *er*.

questions.question_text:
Choose the correct participle.

```text
Ich habe meine Oma gestern ____ .          →  Liguei para minha avó ontem.
```
questions.explanation: *anrufen* is a separable strong verb: the participle is *an + ge + rufen* = *angerufen*, with *ge-* between prefix and stem. In the present the prefix splits off: *Ich rufe sie an.*
